name: Israeli Sign Language
sweep_summary: Israeli Sign Language (isra1236) is not in the catalog. The three Glottolog items are really two works, both by Sandler (with Nespor): 'Prosody in Israeli Sign Language' (Language and Speech 42, 1999; Glottolog lists it twice, once under the preprint title 'Prosodic phonology in ISL' 1998) and 'The medium and the message' (Sign Language & Linguistics 2, 1999). Both were obtained openly from the University of Haifa Sign Language Research Lab media library (signlab.haifa.ac.il; the older sandlersignlab host refuses connections), saved with text extractions under and logged in there; two further Sandler papers from the same site (1999b on cliticization/prosodic words; 2010 TPS overview) were read for completeness. All are about phrasal prosody, not word stress: ISL signs are mostly monosyllabic prosodic words, so no word-internal stress placement is stated anywhere; the papers establish phrase-final prominence (rightmost sign of the phonological phrase, marked by hold/reduplication/pause; intonational-phrase-final by size and slowness) and facial 'intonation'. Nothing remains to acquire (priority none); the DOI landing pages (SAGE, Benjamins) are paywalled but unnecessary. OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Wayback, CORE and BASE were rate-limited or blocked from our machine, so discovery ran through the lab site's WordPress media API and Crossref.

earlier_scan.source_named: Sign language — spoken word stress inapplicable; sign-prosody covered in Meir & Sandler 2008, A Language in Space: The Story of Israeli Sign Language; also hh:phon:Shunary:Israeli-Sign — not open-access

new_statements.quote: if the basic order of ISL is head-complement, as shown in (22), then the rightmost sign of P should be strong and its sister signs weak. This appears to be the case. We are considering the physical correlates of phonological phrase prominence, all realized with the hands, to be the following: hold, reduplication, and pause. [...] All but 30 of the 247 potential phonological phrases had one of these markers on the last word. If these are indeed prominence markers, then the vast majority of phonological phrases in our corpus had prominence at the end.
new_statements.citation: Nespor, Marina & Wendy Sandler (1999). Prosody in Israeli Sign Language. Language and Speech 42(2-3): 143-176 (author preprint from signlab.haifa.ac.il; Glottolog 637032/637033)
new_statements.locator: section 3.2.1 'Grouping and prominence', preprint p. 18 (journal pp. c. 157-158); monosyllabicity of signs at section 2.1, preprint p. 12
new_statements.reading: ISL has no word-stress rule in the spoken-language sense: signs are (mostly) monosyllabic prosodic words (preprint p. 12), so there is no word-internal stress locus, and the authors' own results concern phrase-level prominence only. Prominence falls on the rightmost sign of the phonological phrase (head-complement language), realized manually by hold, reduplication or pause on that sign (216 of 247 phrases), and on the final sign of the intonational phrase by larger, slower signing; focus is marked by moving the focused constituent to I-final position, not by in-situ stress shift (preprint p. 25). If the catalog ever takes sign languages, ISL should be coded 'word stress not applicable (monosyllabic signs); phrasal prominence phrase-final' with this source, not as a fixed or weight-based stress system.

sources.citation: Nespor, Marina and Sandler, Wendy (1999). Prosody in Israeli Sign Language. Language and Speech 42(2-3), 143-176. doi:10.1177/00238309990420020201 [Glottolog 637033]
sources.quote: Summing up thus far, ISL is a language in which the phrasal head precedes its complements, and the basic domain of the phonological phrase extends from the left edge of the syntactic phrase till the head. [...] The prediction of the theory of prosodic phonology is that in a head-complement language such as this one, the most prominent node is the rightmost. Our interpretation of the role of reduplication, hold and pause suggests that this prediction is borne out.
sources.locator: section 3.2.1 (MS pp. 17-18) and 3.2.3 Summary (MS p. 21); Crossref confirms vol. 42 issue 2-3, pp. 143-176, June 1999
sources.note: Duplicate Glottolog record of item 1 (same journal pages; the 1998 'Prosodic phonology...' title is the preprint/lab-site title). Statement of record for prominence in ISL: phrase-final (rightmost sign of the phonological phrase), marked manually by hold, reduplication or pause; intonational-phrase-final prominence by size and slowness; focus is marked by moving the focused constituent to I-final position rather than by stress shift in situ (MS p. 25). Nothing on stress inside the sign/word; signs are monosyllabic.

sources.citation: Nespor, Marina and Sandler, Wendy (1998). Prosodic phonology in Israeli Sign Language. Language and Speech, 143-176. [Glottolog 637032, hhtype phonology]
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.quote: It is generally agreed that the phonology of sign language includes a syllable-like unit and that the movement corresponds to the syllable peak (Coulter 1982; Wilbur 1982; this volume; Brentari 1990, 1999; Perlmutter, 1992; Sandler 1993a). Taken together with constraints on the structure of signs, these observations mean that most signs are monosyllabic. It is argued, in Sandler (1999) that this monosyllabic unit is the optimal form of the prosodic word in sign languages.
sources.locator: author preprint, header 'published in Language & Speech 42: 2&3. 1999. 143-176'; section 2.1 (MS p. 12) and section 3.2.1 'Grouping and prominence' (MS pp. 16-19), 3.2.3 Summary (MS p. 21)
sources.note: Same work as Glottolog 637033 (the lab site files it under the 1998 title; the PDF header gives the published title 'Prosody in Israeli Sign Language', Language and Speech 42(2-3), 1999, 143-176). The paper contains no statement of word-level stress placement: ISL signs are described as (mostly) monosyllabic prosodic words (MS p. 12), so there is no word-internal stress locus to state. What it does establish is PHRASAL prominence: ISL is head-complement, and 'the rightmost sign of P should be strong and its sister signs weak. This appears to be the case' (MS p. 18); the manual correlates of p…

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (2010). Prosody and syntax in sign languages. Transactions of the Philological Society 108(3), 298-328. [not in sweep list; read for stress remarks]
sources.quote: Little is said here about stress / prominence. The reader is referred to Wilbur (1999), Nespor & Sandler (1999), van der Kooij, Crasborn, & Emmerik (2006), and Sandler (to appear a) for investigations and discussions of this issue in different sign languages.
sources.locator: PDF p. 10 (journal p. c. 307), footnote 9; PDF p. 5 footnote 4
sources.note: Later synthesis; explicitly defers stress/prominence to Nespor & Sandler 1999 for ISL. Footnote 4 notes Klima & Bellugi's claim that stress falls on the second member of a compound in ASL (ASL, not ISL). Confirms that Nespor & Sandler 1999 remains the statement of record for ISL prominence.

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (1999a). The medium and the message: Prosodic interpretation of linguistic content in Israeli Sign Language. Sign Language & Linguistics 2(2), 187-215. [Glottolog 643349]
sources.quote: In this preliminary study, it was found that phonological phrases conform to the algorithm in (9), and prominence is at the end, as predicted, since ISL appears to be basically a head-complement language. The correlates of prominence are argued to be reduplication, hold at the end of the prominent sign, or pause after the last word in the phonological phrase.
sources.locator: section 2.1 'The prosodic word' pp. 192-193; section 2.2 'The phonological phrase' pp. 199-200
sources.note: Overview paper (publisher pagination). Introduces the prosodic word in general terms ('The word is also the domain of lexical stress assignment', p. 192) but then discusses ISL prosodic words only through cliticization (coalescence in prominent phrase-final position, handshape assimilation in weak position, pp. 193-197); no rule for stress placement inside an ISL word is given. Restates the Nespor & Sandler finding of phrase-final prominence (p. 199) and reports that lexical reduplication is neutralized by prosodic position (p. 200); the rest is on facial 'superarticulation' as the intonation…

sources.citation: Sandler, Wendy (1999b). Cliticization and prosodic words in a sign language. In T. A. Hall & U. Kleinhenz (eds.), Studies on the Phonological Word, 223-254. Amsterdam: Benjamins. [not in sweep list; found on the Haifa sign-lab site during the sweep]
sources.quote: We discovered the following correlates of rhythmic prominence in ISL, which appears to be a right-branching language: (1) Prominence is marked on the rightmost word of a phonological phrase, mainly by holding the hand still at the end of a sign and/or reduplicating the sign. (2) Prominence is marked on the rightmost word of an intonational phrase with size and rate of signing (large and slow is more prominent).
sources.locator: p. 239 (section on prosodic structure), p. 242, p. 250
sources.note: The closest thing to a word-level stress statement for ISL: pronoun clitics coalesce with a host in phrase-final position 'because the[y] are in a prosodically prominent position but cannot get phrase level stress by themselves' (p. 250), 'on the assumption that stress assignment can only see lexical categories' (p. 242); clitics in weak position 'remain syllabic, but weakly stressed' (p. 250). The prosodic word of ISL is the monosyllabic sign; stress is treated only as phrase-level prominence landing on the phrase-final (lexical) word.
